title: CRLA/362/2004 of ANIL KUMAR Vs STATE

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND
AT NAINITAL
 Criminal Appeal No. 362 of 2004
Anil Kumar .......... Appellant
 versus
State of Uttaranchal .......... Respondent

Ms. Neelima Mishra Joshi, Amicus Curiae, present for the Appellant.
Mr. S.A.Siddiqui, learned AGA, present for the State of Uttarakhand/
Respondent.
 JUDGMENT
Hon'ble U.C. Dhyani, J. (Oral)
. Prosecution story in brief is that PW 2 Km.
Luxmi d/o Pratap Singh was enticed away by accused Anil
Kumar and Ravindra Kumar on 22.07.1998, at 12:00 noon,
from a place within the jurisdiction of PS Sahaspur, District
Dehradun. Kumari Luxmi (victim) was a student of class IX
in Government Inter College, Langha. Anil Kumar was also
student of that school. They were seen by PW 5
Dharmendra Kumar and PW 7 Manoj Kumar. The parents
of the victim made a search for their daughter, but when
they did not succeed in tracing the girl, a first information
report was lodged by PW 1 Pratap Singh on 25.07.1998 at

2
Police Station Sahaspur, at 2:45 p.m. The prosecutrix was
recovered. She was in the company of Anil Kumar. Both of
them were sitting in a drainage on the road leading to
Saharanpur. Recovery memo Ext. Ka-7 was prepared by
PW 7 SI R.S.Tomar. The victim was taken to women
hospital, Dehradun for medical examination. She was
examined by PW 3 Dr. Gopi Bothiyal. On that day, she
refused for her internal medical examination, which
subsequently took place on 29.07.1998.
2. After the investigation, two separate charge
sheets were submitted against the accused persons, namely,
Anil Kumar, Ravindra Kumar and Meera Devi. The case
was committed to the Court of Sessions. When the trial
commenced and prosecution opened it's case, charges for
the offences punishable under Sections 363, 366 and 376(g)
IPC were framed against Anil Kumar and Ravindra Kumar.
A charge under Section 368 IPC read with Section 114 IPC
was framed against accused Meera Devi. The accused
persons pleaded not guilty to the charges framed against
them and claimed trial. Eight witnesses, namely, PW 1
Pratap Singh (father of the victim), PW 2 Km. Luxmi
(victim), PW 3 Dr. Gopi Bouthiyal, PW 4 Dr. B.C.Ramola,
PW 5 Dharmendra, PW 6 Manoj Kumar, PW 7 Rajendra
Singh Tomar and PW 8 Ramesh Chandra were examined on
behalf of the prosecution. Incriminating evidence was put to
the accused persons, in reply to which, they said that they
have been falsely implicated in this case.

3
3. After considering the evidence on record,
learned trial court exonerated Ravindra Kumar and Meera
Devi of the charges levelled against them. Accused-appellant Anil Kumar was found guilty of the offences
punishable under Sections 363 and 376 IPC. He was,
however, acquitted of the charge under Sections 366 IPC.
He was sentenced to undergo three years' rigorous
imprisonment under Section 363 IPC and seven years'
rigorous imprisonment for the offence under Section 376
IPC. Aggrieved against the said conviction and sentence,
present criminal appeal was preferred by the convict
accused Anil Kumar.
4. Prosecution led the evidence through PW 2
Luxmi (victim). In her examination-in-chief, she said that
she was studying in class IX in Government Inter College
Langha two years' ago (from the date of deposition).
Appellant Anil Kumar was also studying in the said school.
On 22.07.1998, she suffered from dysentery. No one was
present in her home. She went to relieve herself in the river.
It was around 1:00 p.m. When she was coming back from
the river, accused persons met her. The appellant and co-accused (Ravindra Kumar) told PW 2 on the knife point to
follow them. PW 2 followed them. Two more boys of the
same village met them, who enquired from the appellant
and the Ravindra as to whether they were going? PW 2
was not allowed to speak. Appellant and Ravindra told the
villagers that they were going to take the books.
Dharmendra and Ravindra, the villagers, went away after

4
the conversation. Appellant and co-accused took PW 2 to
Dakpathar in the house of a woman. That woman served
them with the meals. PW 2 slept in the night. Appellant and
co-accused Ravindra committed rape with her in the night.
The woman gave Rs. 500/- to the appellant and the co-accused. Appellant, co-accused and PW 2 boarded in a bus.
The appellant and the co-accused brought PW 2 to village
Narayan Pur. Accused Meera served them with meals. All
the three took PW 2 to the rooftop. Meera came down in the
ground floor thereafter. Appellant and co-accused
committed rape with PW 2. She remained in the house of
Meera for 2-3 days. On 26.07.1998, Meera again served
them with meals and saw them off. Appellant and co-accused took PW 2 to Saharanpur railway station and said
that they will be going to Delhi. They were intercepted by
the police, but Ravindra was not present with them then.
She was given in the custody of her father. She was taken to
the Magistrate, where her statement under Section 164
Cr.P.C. (Ext. Ka-2) was recorded. When the appellant and
the co-accused committed rape with her in Dakpathhar for
the first time, she was unconscious. PW 2 said that her date
of birth was 12.08.1982. PW 2 was cross-examined, but
nothing came in her cross-examination to suggest that she
was telling a lie.
5. PW 1 Pratap Sngh was the father of PW 1, who
said, among other things, that his daughter's date of birth
was 12th August, 1982. On 24.07.1998, PW 1 received a
phone call. On receiving the said information, he went to

5
his house at village Langha. PW 1 was informed that his
daughter was missing since 22.07.1998. He wrote complaint
(Ext. Ka-1), on the basis of which, the first information
report was lodged. Victim was apprehended from the
possession of the appellant on 28.07.1998 and was given in
the custody of PW 1.
6. PW 5 Dharmendra saw the victim in the
company of the appellant and co-accused on 22.07.1998, at
3:00 p.m. He was witness of having last seen the victim in
the company of the appellant and co-accused. PW 6 Manoj
Kumar, brother of victim, was witness to the recovery of
victim from the possession of the appellant. PW 7 SI
Rajendra Singh Tomar was the investigating officer.
7. The victim was mediclaly examined by PW 3
Dr. Gopi Bauthiyal, Medical Officer, Women's Hospital at
Dehradun on 28.07.1998, at 11:20 a.m. PW 3 proved
medical report (Ext. Ka-3). No mark of external injury was
seen on the victim's body. Initially, the medical officer
reported that no opinion could be given about rape, as
Kumari Luxmi refused to agree for her internal
examination. She (victim), however, gave the consent on
the next day i.e. on 29.7.1998. On her cross-examination,
PW 3 reported that victim's hymen was old torn. No mark
of external injury was found on private parts. Her vagina
admitted two fingers. Vaginal smear was taken and sent for
histopathological examination. In Ext. Ka-4, PW 3 said that
no opinion about rape could be given. In the radiological
report (Ext. Ka-6), radiologist Dr. B.C. Ramola reported

6
that all the epiphysis around elbow joint were fused with
their respective shafts. Lower epiphysis and radius ulna
were not fused with their respective shafts. All epiphysis
around knee joint were fused. All epiphysis around ankle
joint were fused with their respective shafts. On the basis of
fusion in the x-ray, the radiologist found that she was above
16 years and below 17 years.
8. In the pathology report, vaginal smear was found
negative for sperms. On the basis of the report of
pathologist and radiologist, PW 3 submitted supplementary
report (Ext. Ka-5) and opined that the victim was above 16
years but below 18 years of age.
9. The opinions of radiologist and medical officers
are always tentative. They are merely the opinions based on
scientific researches. The controversy about the age of the
victim in the instant case, was set at rest by PW 8 Ramesh,
who was in the ministerial staff of Government Inter
College, Langha, Dehradun. In his examination-in-chief,
PW 8 said that he was posted as clerk in Government Inter
College, Langha since 2002. PW 8 brought Scholars'
Register, which register started from 1994. At serial no.
1936 at page 43, there was an entry of the name of Km.
Luxmi. Her date of birth was also mentioned. PW 8 said
that the date of birth of Km. Luxmi is 12.08.1982. The
signatures of the then Principal of the school were there on
each and every page of the register. PW 8 proved Ext. Ka-23 indicating that the date of birth of the victim as
12.08.1982. By this analogy, she was about 16 years of age

7
on the date of alleged incident. She took admission in the
said college on 15.07.1994. Thus the age of the victim, on
the date of incident, is held to be below 16 years (one
month short of 16 years). Thus the consent, if any, of the
victim was immaterial considering the scheme of Section
375 of IPC, which is reproduced herein below for ready
reference:
375. Rape.- A man is said to commit "rape" who,
except in the case hereinafter excepted, has sexual
intercourse with a woman under circumstances falling
under any of the six following descriptions :-
 First.- ................................
 Secondly.- ....................................
 Thirdly.-..............................
 Fourthly.-............................
 Fifthly.-................................
 Sixthly.- With or without her consent, when she is under sixteen
years of age.
10. Although three defence witnesses were
examined on behalf of the appellant, but the testimony of
those witnesses were in the form of negative evidence. DW
1 to DW 3 thus could not make inroads into the prosecution
story.
11. Learned amicus curiae argued, among other
things, that there was delay in lodging the first information
report. The incident took place on 22.07.1998 and the first
information report was lodged on 27.07.1998 i.e. after five

8
days of the incident. In the first information report, the
names of Anil Kumar and another were mentioned for
enticing away the prosecutrix. Since this Court has to take
into account the case of appellant only at this stage and
therefore, the evidence relating to other accused persons is
being ignored. No purpose will be served by discussing the
evidence which relates to the accused persons other than the
appellant herein. PW 1 Pratap Singh deposed that on
24.07.1998, he got a telephonic message at his work place
in military establishment about his daughter. On receiving
the telephonic message, PW 1 took leave and came to his
village Langha, and then only he came to know about the
incident. When PW 1 came to his village, PW 6 Manoj,
brother of the victim, was not in the village. He had gone to
Himachal Pradesh in the search of his sister. Manoj Kumar
came back on 25.07.1998 and then he told PW 1 about the
involvement of the appellant and co-accused. In the matters
of kidnapping of a minor girl, it is the tendency of the
general people that firstly they make efforts for searching
out the kidnapped girl and then lodge the report, in as much
as, the prestige and status of the family is often at stake.
Thus the delay in lodging the first information report was
satisfactorily explained by the prosecution.
12. Victim, in such cases, is the best witness.
Evidence of the victim has to be relied upon in such cases,
if the evidence is believable. PW 2 (victim) deposed that
when she went to relieve herself in the river and came back,
the accused met her on the river. They put knife on her and

9
took her forcibly. Rape was committed with her, firstly in
Dakpathhar and subsequently, in village Narayan Pur. A
detailed reading of the evidence of the victim reveals that
she was compelled to go with the appellant. Even
otherwise, her consent, if any, was immaterial, in as much
as, she was below 16 years of age. Had she been above 16
years of age and had it been proved that she went with the
appellant on her own volition, the appellant would have
been exonerated of the offence punishable under Section
376 IPC. Even then, there was no chance of acquittal of the
appellant under Section 363 IPC, in as much as, the age of
reckoning for Section 363 IPC is 18 years. In other words,
if the victim is below 18 years, and it is proved that she
went with the accused on her own volition, the same does
not matter, in as much as, the consent of such girl for the
purpose of Section 363 IPC was immaterial, if she was
below 18 years of age.
13. In such view of the matter, the prosecution was
able to prove the case against the appellant for the offences
punishable under Sections 363 and 376 IPC beyond
reasonable doubt. The learned trial court has dealt with each
and every aspect of the prosecution story, which was duly
supported by the prosecution evidence. There is no
illegality in the impugned judgment and order. There is no
question of giving of benefit of doubt to the appellant in the
background of impeccable testimony of the victim, duly
corroborated by the testimony of medical officers and staff
of the Government Inter College, Langha. This Court is

10
unable to take a view contrary to what was taken by the
learned court below.
14. Consequently, the Criminal Appeal is liable to
be dismissed and the same is accordingly dismissed. The
judgment and order dated 06.12.2004 passed by the learned
court below, upholding conviction of the appellant, is
hereby affirmed. The conviction and sentence recorded
against the appellant by the court below is upheld.
Appellant Anil Kumar is on bail. His bail is cancelled. He
is directed to surrender forthwith before the court concerned
to serve out the sentence as was awarded to him by the trial
court and affirmed by this Court.
 Let a copy of this judgment along with the lower
court record be sent to the court concerned for making the
accused-appellant surrender and serve out the sentences as
above.
 (U.C. Dhyani, J.)
Dt. May 27, 2013
Kaushal
